title: US-Iran war: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
description: Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East con
body: Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict."We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours." Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now. The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict. Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression."We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.

schema.headline: US-Iran war: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'

title: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under new rules
description: Pupils will not be allowed to have their phones on them at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.Statutory guidance
body: Pupils will not be allowed to have their phones on them at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.Statutory guidance came into force in June, making schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.Ministers now say changes to that guidance will go beyond the current "no see, no hear" policies in place in some schools - where phones can remain in pupils' bags if they are not seen or heard - when it comes into force from September 2027.But head teachers' unions said schools would struggle to implement stricter new policies without additional funding from government.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government's "clear message" to parents and pupils was that "school is for learning and friendship, not scrolling".Access to phones "risks pulling children away from their learning and from each other", the government said.Schools will be able to decide how to follow the guidance. Some schools have invested in sealed pouches or secure lockers. Others collect phones at the start of the day, or have prohibited them from sites altogether.Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders union, said phones could raise "safety issues" and be an "unhelpful distraction" during the school day. But he said the more robust measures recommended under the new guidance would "come at a cost".Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said the latest guidance "does at least provide some clarity", but added that school leaders "cannot simply make mobile phones disappear"."If all schools are going to be expected to have lockable pouches or other secure storage facilities for every pupil, the cost involved will be very significant indeed," he said."This is not feasible unless the government puts in the funding required to meet these costs."Dame Rachel de Souza, Children's Commissioner for England, said she welcomed strong action to stop phones distracting pupils and disrupting the school day.Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of campaign group of Generation Focus, similarly welcomed the changes, saying "no see, no hear" policies were not working and pupils were still "TikToking in the toilets"."Ultimately, we need to get to a point where it's not normal for every single child to have a personal internet-enabled device in their pockets with them 24/7," she said.Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said she was "delighted that Labour have finally listened to us and agreed to properly ban smartphones in schools".She said it was also the "right thing to do" to have a review of safety standards around the technology used in schools, which the government has also announced on the back of calls for improved guidance.But she criticised what she called a lack of "joined up thinking" over what new tech was being allowed in classrooms.Because education is devolved, the approach to phones in schools varies across the UK.In Scotland, external, the government has said it will introduce a new law to restrict the personal use of phones in schools, and launched a consultation on the issue over the summer.In Wales, external, the Senedd recently voted against a motion to introduce a national statutory ban on phones in classrooms. Schools are still encouraged to restrict the use of phones during the school day, but heads have flexibility over how to implement their own rules.And in Northern Ireland, Education Minister Paul Givan launched a 12-week consultation in August on whether to ban mobile phones from schools by law, calling for "a stronger and more consistent approach across our education system".Rules around phones in schools are separate from the UK's upcoming ban on social media for under-16s, due to be introduced in March.Children will be barred from accessing platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Vinted and eBay could also be included in the list of platforms set to be banned, the culture secretary has said.Additional reporting by Beth Rose and Nathan Standley

schema.headline: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under new rules

title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
description: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform t
body: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action. Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process."I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.  In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest. In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December."It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says."I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

schema.headline: I took Vinted to court to get my money back

title: 'Cruise for life' ship Villa Vie Odyssey seized in Singapore
description: A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore. The Odys
body: A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore. The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said."Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website. "For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

schema.headline: 'Cruise for life' ship Villa Vie Odyssey seized in Singapore

title: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of violence and abuse against her
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jemima Goldsmith (left) and Russell Brand (right) dated for about a year in the mid-2010sByAleks PhillipsUpda
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jemima Goldsmith (left) and Russell Brand (right) dated for about a year in the mid-2010sByAleks PhillipsUpdated 2 hours agoWarning - this report contains graphic content.Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.Goldsmith, who dated the disgraced entertainer for roughly a year around 2014, alleged that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.In a lengthy statement on social media, the 52-year-old said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison earlier on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.He was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women. The judge at the sentencing hearing told Brand that he harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.The mother-of-two said she had chosen not to pursue legal recourse against Brand over the alleged violent incident in 2014 as she was "worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children".She wrote on X on Monday evening: "Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."Goldsmith said she had not seen nor spoken to Brand since 2014, but claimed to have assisted the journalists who exposed the allegations against him and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" were they sued.In her statement, she also addressed reports of an injunction taken out by her and Brand in October 2015 that banned a woman, Szilvia Berki, from harassing them including by making allegations of assault by Brand at Goldsmith's home the prior year.Goldsmith said on Monday that Berki had visited her house for roughly 30 minutes on 7 June 2014 to give Brand a massage, which she said did not end up taking place once she arrived.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jemima Goldsmith (pictured) alleged she once had to call the police on BrandGoldsmith said that Berki later told police that Brand had pushed her in the back while she had been leaving and that she had been attacked by Goldsmith's dog. Brand's ex-girlfriend said she "did not see anything untoward" during the encounter.She added that, after providing a statement and CCTV footage, police concluded that there was no case to answer.Goldsmith accused Berki of then sending a series of "vicious antisemitic and threatening" messages and posting "wild and untrue allegations" about her on social media.She said she then agreed to a suggestion from Brand's lawyer to seek an injunction to prevent harassment. She claimed on Monday that recent media reporting of the injunction had opened her up "to vile hatred and abuse online".Sunday Times chief news correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023, has told the BBC that Goldsmith helped her "a lot"."I have seen the abuse she's been getting online and I did try to tell people that part of the story was much more complicated than they realise," Urwin said. "I wish people would remember women that come forward are brave people and that is what she has done tonight – she has spoken out with immense bravery about how Russell Brand treated her," she added.Brand's sentencing hearing heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.One of them said she was "upset and traumatised" for years after the incident, adding: "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."The woman he was found guilty of raping said the trauma was something she had to "carry every day".A van believed to be carrying Brand was seen arriving at HMP Wandsworth in London on Monday after the sentencing hearing.The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case, that would be seven years.Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag. The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009 following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court.He was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

schema.headline: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of violence and abuse against her

title: Early prisoner release: More offenders to leave jail on Tuesday
description: Around 650 more offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on Tuesday in the third phase of the government's plan to end the prison population cr
body: Around 650 more offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on Tuesday in the third phase of the government's plan to end the prison population crisis.The group will include offenders serving up to three years and two months for their crimes.Under the new rules, they are leaving jail after serving no more than a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than a half.At least 1,350 offenders have left jail early since 1 October under the first two waves of the scheme.By the end of the year officials project that at least 2,500 will have been let out to spend two-thirds of their sentence on a licence in the community.Tuesday's third stage continues the process of releasing batches of offenders serving increasingly long sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years.The cohort will include people convicted of affray, which has a maximum sentence of three years, burglary and fraud. Some violent offenders convicted of wounding, grievous bodily harm with intent or lower-end firearms charges could also be released.Offenders convicted of one of more than 70 offences are exempt from the earlier release scheme, including manslaughter, rape, sexual and grooming offences and those on life terms.Weekly prison population statistics show that the early release programme is having an impact - for now - on the population crisis inside jails.On Monday the latest release of weekly data showed there were 86,982 people in jail, with enough spare spaces to take in 2,076 additional offenders if needs be. That is 500 more cells available at any one time than was the case on the eve of the programme beginning in October.Victims' groups and survivors have also raised concerns. Refuge, which supports survivors of domestic abuse, told the BBC last month that perpetrators of such abuse were among those being released.Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence. Once outside, they will be monitored by probation officers, who are responsible for trying to make sure that offenders take part in courses or other programmes to turn around their lives - and also that they keep to their licence conditions, which can include bans on entering certain areas and contacting victims.The government has not yet published any figures for the rate of recall of prisoners to jails for breaching their licence conditions.The most up to date statistics show that just 12,338 offenders were sent back to jail for breaching their terms between April and June. That was 12% higher than the year before but a decrease on the first three months of the year.Rehabilitation experts say that the recalls are often more likely to be linked to the offender failing to keep to appointments or living at a specific address. Around a fifth of recalls are for a new offence.Napo, the probation service union, has previously said the releases have put enormous strain on its members who are charged with monitoring the offenders in the community.Its members have been balloted over recent weeks on potential strike action over pay and conditions - and the result of that poll is expected on Friday.The government has offered probation officers a 5% pay rise by the Ministry of Justice, while it had demanded 12% as part of a plan to make up for loss of earnings caused by cuts from 2010.The Ministry of Justice says the offer is fair and has been accepted by two other unions and is twinned with a £700m investment in probation to recruit 1,300 extra officers and the roll-out of AI tools to cut the workload of monitoring offenders.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has previously criticised the scheme, saying she was "worried about dangerous people being let out on the street when they haven't served their sentence, haven't been rehabilitated".An early release programme introduced by the Conservatives saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024.

schema.headline: Early prisoner release: More offenders to leave jail on Tuesday

title: Booker Prize 2026: M John Harrison's 'baffling but brilliant' novel The End of Everything wins
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, M John Harrison was billed by Booker bosses as "a genuinely original thinker"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterAuth
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, M John Harrison was billed by Booker bosses as "a genuinely original thinker"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterAuthor M John Harrison has become the oldest ever winner of the Booker Prize, picking up the prestigious literary award for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything.Harrison, 81, who has built a cult following over his 60-year career, was named the winner of the £50,000 prize at a ceremony in London on Monday.The End of Everything is set in the years after a mysterious catastrophe that caused British society as we know it to collapse. It has divided opinion among readers, and was described as "bleak but brilliant" and "dreamlike and baffling" by one critic.Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the Booker judges, said: "It's a challenging read, but some of the best fiction is challenging."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Harrison (far left) with his fellow nominees (left-right) Elizabeth Strout, Luke Kennard, Rebecca Perry, Marlon James and Douglas StuartDame Mary added: "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism."Harrison began writing in the 1960s and has published 13 novels, five short story collections and an "anti-memoir". He has now surpassed Margaret Atwood as the oldest ever Booker winner.While he dislikes labels like science fiction and fantasy, he has been called "the titan of literary science fiction", and Booker Prize chief executive Gaby Wood said he is "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world"."He is a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously," Wood said."Though very unsettling, The End of Everything is not in fact a strange book. It's a realist book about a strange world, populated by desperate, unmoored characters."Listen back to a special edition of BBC Radio 4 Front Row from the Booker Prize ceremony'Tender, terrifying and timely'The story follows a man and his aunt who must muddle through on the south-east English coast in the aftermath of an unexplained disaster and the arrival of mysterious alien beings.The author has said he deliberately omitted as much explanation about the background to the events as possible, in order to make readers feel the same disorientation as the characters.He has said: "The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It's a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend."He added: "I've passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien."That approach has led to a mixed reaction. The Guardian praised the book but said, external "it won't be for everyone", while the New York Times said, external: "The more we learn about the conditions of this novel's broken world, the harder it is to grasp."The Literary Review described it as, external "a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts", while the Telegraph said, external "you feel you're not so much reading as dreaming".Another Telegraph critic wrote, external that it was "ultimately, in both skill and humour, a cut above" the other shortlisted books."And in an age when AI overlords keep threatening to kill us, and the Government has told us to stockpile tinned food and bottled water, it is, for once, a novel that you can genuinely call 'timely'."The Booker Prize is an annual award for the best novel written in the English language and published in the year up to 30 September. It was launched in 1969.This year's other shortlisted books were:The Disappearers by Marlon JamesBlack Bag by Luke KennardMay We Feed the King by Rebecca PerryThe Things We Never Say by Elizabeth StroutJohn of John by Douglas StuartWhen the shortlist was announced in September, Dame Mary said agreeing on the final six had been, "to put it mildly, hard work".Another judge, US novelist Patricia Lockwood, said she had been "tossing books across the room" during judging sessions, while poet Raymond Antrobus described the selection as "a tussle".The other judges were Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, and journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu.Speaking about the final judging session, Dame Mary told reporters on Monday:  "There was a lot of discussion, disagreement and debate. But nobody stomped off."In a statement, she said the panel "spent a whole day debating the six remarkable novels on this year's shortlist" before reaching a unanimous decision to name Harrison the winner.

schema.headline: Booker Prize 2026: M John Harrison's 'baffling but brilliant' novel The End of Everything wins

title: England: Kane and Bellingham air strong views in World Cup review
description: The ramifications of the Argentina defeat, or perhaps more pertinently, the circumstances, meant some of the squad held grievances, with those feeling
body: The ramifications of the Argentina defeat, or perhaps more pertinently, the circumstances, meant some of the squad held grievances, with those feelings lingering and even growing throughout the summer.In particular there was unhappiness about how Tuchel told them to approach the closing stages of the game after Anthony Gordon had given them a 55th-minute advantage.Enzo Fernandez struck an equaliser with five minutes left, before Lautaro Martinez headed in a stoppage-time winner.As reported by BBC Sport at the time, a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive.Hindsight, of course, is 20/20. England appeared to retreat in the closing stages of the last-16 tie against Mexico earlier in the tournament - but successfully defended a 3-2 lead to reach the quarter-finals to trigger scenes of joy at the iconic Azteca Stadium.Nevertheless, certain players felt let down by the team's apparent pragmatism during the closing stages of the loss to Argentina amid a sense that going for the South Americans' jugular would have provided greater success.Inevitably, the game against Argentina emerged as a key theme at the squad discussion.It is understood that Tuchel pointed to the quality of the opposition as a key factor on why they eventually succumbed to two late Argentina goals.There is, of course, merit to that argument. Lionel Messi was in the opposition team after all.That said, it was not an argument the players in the meeting were prepared to universally accept.There is a strongly held view within the England squad that their team, man-for-man, was superior to Argentina, who had 38-year-old Nicolas Otamendi on the field for the closing 18 minutes of the game.All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting.As you would expect, captain Harry Kane was strong and forthright with his views.Jude Bellingham, too, is said to have been particularly candid in expressing his belief that this current crop of England players were more than capable of continuing to take the game to Argentina.Bellingham's contribution to the meeting is said to have underlined his growing influence within the England squad, with many believing the Real Madrid midfielder will become the team's captain once Kane is no longer in the picture.If the air needed to be cleared after the World Cup then it appears those honest discussions at the end of September did the trick.Barring the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley in their first Nations League fixture in September, England have bounced back from the loss to Argentina emphatically - scoring 12 goals without conceding in three fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia.Similarly, the fluctuating relationship between Bellingham and Tuchel seems to have improved, too."It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place," Tuchel said last week."I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways."We will get a clearer idea of how 'Tuchel 2.0' is progressing in the next few days when England host Croatia on Thursday and travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday.

schema.headline: England: Kane and Bellingham air strong views in World Cup review

title: Ukraine peace talks resume in Abu Dhabi after months-long pause
description: Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario
body: Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said.The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February.Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches.Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine."An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart.A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture"."They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans." Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe".Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said."While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations.""This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

schema.headline: Ukraine peace talks resume in Abu Dhabi after months-long pause

title: Ben White: England defender says people don't know 'full story' behind his self-inflicted exile from national team
description: Arsenal defender Ben White says people do not know the "full story" behind his decision to previously make himself unavailable for England selection -
body: Arsenal defender Ben White says people do not know the "full story" behind his decision to previously make himself unavailable for England selection - but says he would make the same decision again.White, who has been named in Thomas Tuchel's squad for upcoming Nations League fixtures, left the Three Lions' camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to return home for personal reasons.He then made himself unavailable for selection for the rest of Gareth Southgate's reign, and was booed by some fans in March's 1-1 draw with Ukraine after returning to the squad under Tuchel.Asked by BBC Radio 5 live's football correspondent John Murray what he would say to people who define his England career by what happened in Qatar, White said: "I think obviously people don't know the full story, because I [have] never said anything and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that."I think that is probably the best way."It's been amazing [though], obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it is amazing to be here now."White is now 29 and asked if he would have done anything differently in hindsight, he added: "No, I don't think I would."Obviously, I was a bit younger, I am a bit older now."I think as a person I am quite real and I think I made the decision that I would probably continue to make."So, one that I am not happy about, but obviously it happened and [it is] time to move on."White came on for his first England appearance since 2022 in March's 1-1 draw with Uruguay and was booed by some supporters before he scored but also gave away the penalty that led to the visitors' equaliser.After that, Chelsea midfielder Jordan Henderson said he and his fellow England players would always support White, while Tuchel said recently that the defender deserves "a new chapter" and "positive feedback from the crowd".Asked how he dealt with the emotions of that night at Wembley, White added: "Before the game I was thinking 'don't not stand out, but [take it] nice and easy'."Then I came on and obviously got booed, then I scored, then I gave away a penalty."So, it was obviously full of emotions that night, [but] it was a good night."England play Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November before taking on world champions Spain in Madrid three days later.White is looking to add to his six England caps in this international break and said: "It is obviously an amazing privilege to be called up."The feeling is the same every time you do get this chance to play for England. It's one I am really looking forward to this week."

schema.headline: Ben White: England defender says people don't know 'full story' behind his self-inflicted exile from national team

title: WTA Finals: Aryna Sabalenka beats Karolina Muchova in first group match
description: Aryna Sabalenka grappled with her own frustrations and a misfiring serve to begin her WTA Finals campaign with a tight victory over Karolina Muchova.W
body: Aryna Sabalenka grappled with her own frustrations and a misfiring serve to begin her WTA Finals campaign with a tight victory over Karolina Muchova.World number two Sabalenka is bidding to win the season-ending title for the first time in her sixth appearance.With rival and world number one Elena Rybakina withdrawing on the eve of the competition, Sabalenka is arguably the favourite to triumph on the courts where she won the Indian Wells title in March.However, neither she nor Wimbledon runner-up Muchova were consistently at their best in the first group two match.Belarus' Sabalenka battled back from a break down in both sets to win 7-6 (7-2) 7-5.She cut a frustrated figure at times but reined in her emotions, with her forehand in particular growing stronger as the match progressed.Her serve, however, was inconsistent. Sabalenka produced seven double faults to four aces, but landed 59% of her first serves and won 33 of 44 points behind it."It was a bit tricky with the sun [and] with the shade," Sabalenka told Sky Sports."Sometimes I had to adjust my toss, sometimes I had to serve blind, but it's all part of the game."French Open champion Mirra Andreeva was far more convincing in a 6-4 6-0 victory over Ukraine's Elina Svitolina later on Monday.Sabalenka has had - by her high standards - a strange season.For the first time since 2022 she has not won a Grand Slam singles title, having lost the Australian Open and US Open finals to Rybakina, and her last title came in Miami in March.After winning just one of her three matches during the Asian swing, Sabalenka took a break before the season-ending finals.She faced a tricky task against the crafty Muchova, who was the only player at the event to have a winning head-to-head against her.The Czech also claimed the first break of the opening set - but, in a pattern that repeated throughout the match, Sabalenka broke straight back.Muchova served for the first set but a string of errors forced her into a tie-break, and more mistakes gifted Sabalenka the opener.A topsy-turvy second set featured five breaks of serve, with Sabalenka serving the match out on her second attempt.Teenager Andreeva, who beat Sabalenka in the 2025 Indian Wells final, was ruthless against Svitolina.The Russian reeled off seven games in a row against the wayward Svitolina, backed by her impressive backhand.Andreeva saved all six break points she faced - four of which came in the final game - and hit nine winners to 12 unforced errors in a 77-minute victory.Elsewhere, Britain's Cameron Norrie beat Australian James Duckworth 7-5 6-0 to reach the Stockholm Open second round.Norrie will face top seed Taylor Fritz next as he continues his preparations for this month's Davis Cup Finals.Fellow Briton Toby Samuel claimed a 6-3 6-2 win over Leo Borg - son of 11-time Grand Slam singles champion Bjorn - at the same event.

schema.headline: WTA Finals: Aryna Sabalenka beats Karolina Muchova in first group match

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Brand jailed for 10 years' and 'shamed star caged'
description: Most of Tuesday's papers lead with the sentencing of the comedian Russell Brand after his conviction on charges of rape and sexual assault.The Guardia
body: Most of Tuesday's papers lead with the sentencing of the comedian Russell Brand after his conviction on charges of rape and sexual assault.The Guardian, external, Daily Express, external and Daily Star, external all quote the judge's sentencing remarks, in which he called Brand a "predator". The i Paper, external picks out another part of judge Joel Bennathan's speech; when he described the comedian as "staggeringly arrogant". Metro, external's front page features a picture of Brand, and below it one of his wife leaving court on Tuesday. "Still no remorse" reads the Sun, external's headline, while the Daily Mirror, external's says simply "10 years". The Daily Mail, external reports Brand is facing new abuse claims. The paper says police have received multiple reports of sexual abuse since the 51-year-old was convicted last week.The Financial Times, external leads on Nvidia shares falling sharply after the tech firm said it would investigate claims its chief executive, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. £350bn was wiped off the company's market value at one point, according to the paper. The Guardian says President Trump and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, have thrown their support behind Huang. The Nvidia chief has admitted being "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised.Cabinet Secretary Dame Antonia Romeo will today use her first speech in the role to call for a reimagining of the civil service, according to the Daily Telegraph, external. It reports that she will say changes are needed to address low public trust in the government, and the emergence of AI. The paper says her plans represent "the biggest overhaul of the British state in more than 170 years".The Times, external says researchers believe the gap between humans and chimpanzees may be smaller than previously thought. It reports that a team of scientists have found young chimps learn to speak by listening to and mimicking their elders. The study's lead author is quoted as saying their findings suggest "there is still much to discover" about the primates.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Brand jailed for 10 years' and 'shamed star caged'

title: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor
description: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the
body: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home."My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models."My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women. Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, externalAn email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier. "Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims."Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action LineLawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves."These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times."People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward."There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."Additional reporting by Annika Grosser

schema.headline: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor

title: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
description: Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environmen
body: Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week – more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid £350,000.Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain.But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs until September 2023 when he left the Civil Service.He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of Civil Service databases, such as payroll, every two years to look for anomalies.On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence".Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him.He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head.He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box. Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013.He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system. However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long?Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication.Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said. "That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs."There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country.Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her.But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP.In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period.His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job – this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere.Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs.Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems.But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years.In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than £40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including £45,000 in premium bonds.A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management."Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said. "But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement."A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost £285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions."This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account."The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers". Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue.He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark.Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home.The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered £500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months. Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her £2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it.At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer.Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence.

schema.headline: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long

title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
description: Figure caption, "He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen HuangByMichael Race and Osmond ChiaBusiness reportersUpdated 1 hour
body: Figure caption, "He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen HuangByMichael Race and Osmond ChiaBusiness reportersUpdated 1 hour agoUS President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign."I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off its value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the investigation, or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday. The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China." The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.'He said he had no idea she was a spy'At the White House, Trump was asked several times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific. Trump said he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations."I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today. Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.Additional reporting by Tessa Wong in Singapore

schema.headline: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
